newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airlines' Q1 earnings expected to soar.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airlines' Q1 earnings expected to soar.

text.p: U.S. airlines are expected to post strong first quarter results, flying high on strong demand, solid pricing and controlled capacity growth, industry analysts said.

Delta Air Lines Inc and UAL Corp's United Airlines are expected to be the clear winners this quarter, while Trans World Airlines Inc and ValuJet Inc are still suffering from lingering cost problems, they said.
"It should be a great quarter for the airline industry. Anything that could go right did go right," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst with Lehman Brothers.

"Earnings for everyone are coming going to come in really great. Delta is going to have a superb quarter, United is having a sensational quarter," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read.

The 10 major U.S. airlines are expected to post a total net profit of $642 million in the first quarter, up sharply from $156 million last year, said Susan Donofrio, an analyst with NatWest Securities. Operating revenues will be about $20.5 billion, up 8.1 percent from $18.9 billion last year.
Airlines culled extra revenues from January 1 to March 7 by pocketing the 10 percent passenger excise tax that would normally go to the federal government.

Labor woes overshadowed the quarter, as American Airlines battled its pilots union in a showdown that caused President Clinton to react. After months of fruitless negotiations, American's pilots went on strike in mid-February, only to be immediately sent back to work by a Presidential Emergency Board created to resolved the dispute.

The pilots' board recently approved a tenative agreement reached with AMR Corp's management which offers a nine percent percent wage increase. The rank and file union members still must ratify the pact, which allows pilots from the airline's American Eagle unit to fly regional jets American is set to buy.

Although American's pilot strike was brief, the airline still lost money as passengers booked away from the airline to avoid being stranded by a possible strike. Airlines such as United and Delta were the main beneficiaries of American's woes, picking up extra passengers and goodwill.
United Airlines also resolved contract disputes with its pilots and mechanics, but US Airways Group Inc remains mired in slow negotiations with its pilots.
US Airways should post solid first quarter profits, its high operating expenses continue to dampen its earnings potential, analysts said.
While the airline sector remains strong overall, Northwest Airlines Corp's first quarter earnings could be somewhat disappointing compared to the sector due to the weaker yen, analysts said.

Meanwhile, TWA faces serious cash flow problems, analysts said. The St. Louis-based carrier said its cash balance of $181.6 million at the end of 1996 is only half of the cash balance the year before.

TWA warned that its first quarter operating loss will exceed last year's operating loss of $54.2 million. The company's expected shortfall comes amid a warning from its auditors that the company may have trouble continuing as a "going concern."
